$comment: The faces a run's characters fall back to when its own face (and that face's open stand-in) has no glyph for them, by script, in the order a font stack lists them. One table for every surface that draws text: the presentation stacks (script-fallbacks.ts), the print page (the same stacks in the server's browser) and the census font-coverage leg (MRAI-corpus/pptx-fast/look/font_cover.py), so what the coverage metric calls covered is what the page draws.

Why (census rounds 31-83, 2179 decks, 11.9 M characters, 10-22): 2.3 % of the characters decks draw are ones their face's stand-in has no glyph for -- Arial's Arabic (Arimo has none: 71 k characters), Cambria's Cyrillic (Caladea has none: 44 k), Calibri's Telugu and Gurmukhi, Hangul and emoji in Latin runs. Office draws them from the named face itself or from its own linked fallback; the page drew whatever the reader's machine had (a CJK face for Cyrillic under a zh locale, a missing-glyph box on the print server).

Order: the Latin family's own extension first (Latin Extended, Greek, Cyrillic, Vietnamese), then the complex scripts, then emoji (in colour, as Office's Segoe UI Emoji draws them), symbols and math, East Asian last: a Han face ahead of the others would draw the Latin-script punctuation it also carries (full-width quotes, the 10-22 audit's 'quotes drawn wide').

East Asian ambiguous punctuation (U+2018-201D quotes, U+2026 ellipsis, U+2014 em dash, U+00B7) is not a fallback question: DrawingML gives a run three slots by character (ECMA-376 21.1.2.3.7/.3/.1), and these characters are Latin-slot characters whatever the run's language (app/services/document_font_face.font_slot_for_codepoint, officeFontScriptSlots.ts). A run's Latin face draws them; where that face is a Chinese Office face, its metric stand-in carries them at the Office face's own advances (cjk-latin-advances.json).
